claim: FIB-SEM can automatically generate 3D images with superior z-axis resolution.

claim: Moderate positive bias transforms a traditional in-column (InLens) detector into an effective backscattered electron detector.
source: This scheme transforms a traditional in-column (InLens) detector into an effective backscattered electron detector that captures a larger fraction of the backscattered electrons, resulting a ~ 10x improvement of imaging speed without contrast degradation compared to a traditional energy-selective backscattered (EsB) detector alone (see Figure 11j).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results and discussion section with reference to Figure 11j.

claim: Moderate positive bias results in a ~ 10x improvement of imaging speed without contrast degradation compared to a traditional energy-selective backscattered (EsB) detector alone.

claim: Biological volumes as large as 1 million µm3 containing biologically meaningful neuronal elements can now be routinely acquired in a few months.

claim: The Drosophila optic lobe was imaged at 8 × 8 × 8 nm3 voxel resolution over a 100 day period.

evidence: This is stated directly in the Results and discussion section with reference to Figure 3.

claim: The Drosophila optic lobe imaging yielded a final four terabyte image volume of about 180 × 100 × 50 µm3.

claim: SEM imaging is usually slower than that of transmission electron microscopy (TEM).

source: First, SEM acquires images pixel-by-pixel in series, whereas TEM acquires all pixels of the image in parallel, with orders of magnitude larger imaging current.

claim: The low SEM landing energy of <2 keV typically used to reduce the electron penetration depth into the block-face can reduce contrast, especially below 800 eV.

claim: For resolution of <10 nm at low landing energy, the incoming electron beam current must be limited to <10 nA.
source: Fourth, the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of a pixel depends on the number of primary electrons devoted to it, which in turn is determined by the beam current. For resolution of <10 nm at low landing energy, the incoming electron beam current must be limited to <10 nA, since higher current beams require larger apertures, which are subject to greater spherical and chromatic aberrations as well as Coulomb repulsion, creating unacceptable blur in the beam spot.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Technology and methods section as a constraint on beam current.

claim: Epon, a common epoxy embedding compound, develops streaks and uneven milling especially downstream on the milled surface.

claim: A positive bias of the specimen above 500 eV can more directly and effectively filter out low-energy secondary electrons that are detected by the InLens detector.

claim: The positively biased InLens image eliminates the rectangular electron burn spot.

claim: The bias enables the InLens detector to offer much improved material contrast, with a ~5–10x gain on electron counts compared to EsB alone.

claim: The ratio of InLens detected electrons to the number of backscattered electrons provides an alternate measure of detection efficiency.

claim: The experimentally determined ratio of backscattered current to primary current is ~27% for gold.

claim: The measured InLens current is about half of the total backscatter current (55% detector efficiency at 1.2 keV).

evidence: This is stated directly in the Technology and methods section with reference to Figure 15.
